Hinton said he left a recent closed-door briefing with 19 U.S. senators “maybe a little bit more optimistic,” though he noted the group was largely self-selected, with 17 Democrats attending. He said physicist

raised the idea that AI should be regulated the way drugs are, requiring companies to prove safety to a government body, similar to the FDA, before release. Hinton agreed that “seems like the very least we should have for AI.”

Asked whether such oversight could realistically move fast enough, Hinton pointed to the climate-change precedent, saying meaningful political pressure only built once the public understood the stakes. He said the same shift is “beginning” with AI.
